sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section introduces the verse "And I will return in peace to my father's house" and raises several questions about its precise wording and sequence.

translations.translation: "And I will return in peace to my father's house, etc."1
[This verse is the beginning of the first discourse of our parshah in Torah Ohr by the Alter Rebbe and in Toras Chayim by the Mitteler Rebbe, the Baal HaGeulah
(of Yud Kislev)2
and the Hillula
(of the 9th of Kislev).
However, in Toras Chayim he prefaces
(at the beginning of the discourse)
the verse3
"And Yaakov vowed a vow, etc." which precedes the verse "And I will return in peace, etc."],
And the precise points in this are known,
What is the meaning of his saying "And I will return in peace to my father's house,"
specifically "in peace"4.
And especially that before this3
he says "If G-d will be with me, etc. and give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,"
that the intention in this is also for bread and clothing in a spiritual sense5,
in all the interpretations of this,
and nevertheless he is not satisfied with this and emphasizes that his return to his father's house will specifically be in peace.
And also one must understand what after "And I will return in peace to my father's house" he adds "and HaVaYaH will be to me for a G-d,"
for this matter that HaVaYaH is the G-d is an essential and constant matter
(as explained in many places6),
and what is the novelty in the above
(and the elevation)
in "and HaVaYaH will be to me for a G-d"7,
and especially after "And I will return in peace to my father's house."
And also one must understand what is said afterwards8
"and this stone which I have set as a pillar shall be a house of G-d,"
how can it be that a stone, which is inanimate
[for even after all the elevations in it
(by means of "which I have set as a pillar")
it is still called a stone,
a level of inanimate]
will be on such a lofty level that it will be a house of G-d9.
And it is explained in the discourses10
that the explanation of "and HaVaYaH will be to me for a G-d" is that a higher light will be drawn down,
such that relative to this light,
HaVaYaH
(of now)
will be
(only)
a level of Elokim.
And the explanation of "and this stone, etc. shall be a house of G-d"
(which comes after and in continuation of "and HaVaYaH will be to me for a G-d")
is that the stone will be a house for the G-d that will be then,
for HaVaYaH that will be for a G-d.
Based on this, further explanation is needed as to how it is possible that the stone,
an inanimate object,
will be a house for this G-d.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the narrative of Yaakov's vow provides an eternal lesson and empowerment for every Jew, connected to the concept of "Vayetzei."

translations.translation: B)
Now, since the Torah is eternal11,
it is understood,
that the matter of "And Yaakov vowed a vow, etc." is a lesson for every single Jew in all places and in all times.
And moreover,
since "the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children"12,
the lesson from the matter of "And Yaakov vowed a vow, etc." is
(like all the matters of the deeds of the fathers)
with greater intensity and greater strength.
[And from this it is understood,
that also the empowerment within this lesson is not merely a general empowerment,
like all lessons of the Torah
(which are also an empowerment13),
but a special empowerment,
since this lesson is from the deeds of the fathers,
and the deeds of the fathers are
(not only a sign,
but also)
an empowerment14
for the children].
And since "And Yaakov vowed a vow, etc." comes in continuation of "And Yaakov went out"15
from Be'er Sheva, etc.
[as is also understood simply,
that the request "And I will return in peace to my father's house" is related to "And he went out, etc."
For because he went out from Be'er Sheva
(and his father's house)
therefore he asked that he should return and go back there,
and that his return should be in peace],
it is understood from this,
that so too regarding the lesson for every single Jew from "And Yaakov vowed a vow, etc."
[and from the request "And I will return in peace to my father's house, etc."],
that this relates to the matter of "And he went out, etc. from Be'er Sheva" as it is in every single Jew.
